questions.question: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase, and when do you use each?
questions.title: Git Merge Vs Rebase
questions.direct_answer: Merge creates a merge commit joining two histories — history is preserved as it happened, nothing is rewritten; use for shared branches (feature → main). Rebase replays your commits onto a new base — history becomes linear and clean, but commit SHAs are rewritten; use on YOUR OWN unpushed branch to update it, never on branches others may have. Squash-merge (the common team policy): rebase-clean history with merge's safety.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Merge creates a merge commit joining two histories — history is preserved as it happened, nothing is rewritten; use for shared branches (feature → main). Rebase replays your commits onto a new base — history becomes linear and clean, but commit SHAs are rewritten; use on YOUR OWN unpushed branch to update it, never on branches others may have. Squash-merge (the common team policy): rebase-clean history with merge's safety.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The mechanics, stated precisely:

```
MERGE (git checkout main && git merge feature)
  before:  main: A—B—C        after:  A—B—C———M   (M = merge commit)
           feature: D—E                 \—D—E/
  history: TRUE — 'D and E happened on a branch, merged at M'
  rewrites: NOTHING. Safe on shared branches.

REBASE (git checkout feature && git rebase main)
  before:  main: A—B—C        after:  main: A—B—C
           feature: D—E                 feature: D'—E'  (REPLAYED)
  history: LINEAR — the commits now sit atop C as if written there
  rewrites: the SHAs of D,E (D→D', E→E'). DANGEROUS if anyone else has D,E.
```

The decision rules (the interview answer):
- Shared branch (others pulled it): MERGE only. Rewriting shared history breaks everyone's clones (their D,E become 'different' commits; merges get duplicated).
- Your local, unpushed branch updating from main: REBASE — you get clean linear history with zero coordination cost. The golden rule: rebase freely before push, never after.
- Team policy options (name them): merge-commits (full history — GitLab-style), squash-merge (one commit per PR — GitHub default; the PR becomes ONE well-written commit on main; reviewable diffs stay in the PR), rebase-merge (linear, per-commit). Squash is the pragmatic favorite: messy WIP history stays in the PR, main sees only squashed intent.

The conflict difference (the practical detail): both can hit conflicts. Merge: resolve ONCE in the merge commit. Rebase: resolve PER REPLAYED COMMIT (feature has 10 commits, each may conflict) — the escape hatch is git rebase -i with squash/fixup to shrink the replay set first.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph merge
        M1[A-B-C on main] --> MC[M merge commit]
        M2[D-E on feature] --> MC
    end
    subgraph rebase
        R1[A-B-C base] --> RP[D' E' replayed — linear]
    end
    S{branch shared?}
    S -->|yes| MERGE[merge only — never rewrite]
    S -->|no, local only| REB[rebase before push]
    POLICY[squash-merge: 1 PR = 1 clean commit on main]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
What rebase actually does (the internals): it finds the merge-base, computes the diff of each of your commits, checks out the new base, and APPLIES each diff as a new commit (new committer timestamp, new SHA — the author info carries over). It's cherry-pick in a loop. This is why rebased commits are NEW objects: 'same changes, different commits' — and why a rebase of a branch with a commit that was already merged upstream shows as conflicts or duplicates: content exists twice with different identities.

Interactive rebase (the power tool): git rebase -i lets you pick/squash/fixup/reword/reorder commits BEFORE sharing. The professional workflow: build a feature as 15 WIP commits, then -i squash into 2-3 reviewable ones with real messages, then push. fixup commits (commit --fixup + rebase -i --autosquash) let you 'patch that typo' without a new commit polluting the branch.

The reflog safety net (the recovery story everyone should know): 'lost' commits from a bad rebase/reset aren't gone — git reflog records every HEAD movement for ~90 days; git reset --hard HEAD@{n} or a branch checkout recovers the pre-rebase state. This is what makes rebase safe to practice: the escape hatch is always there. The close that lands: merge preserves truth, rebase writes the story you wish had happened — choose by whether anyone else has read the history, not by aesthetics.
